header.name: Theories of Ethics
header.description:
The history of Ethics in the western philosophical tradition has witnessed a fundamental shift in its set of concerns and its basic approach in modernity that marks a ‘decisive break’ in relation to its point of departure in ancient Greek thought. This shift, broadly characterized, consists in moving from the question of what constitutes a ‘good life’—one that is conducive to the fullest realization of human potentiality, to what constitutes ‘right’ or ‘wrong’ action.
This course will articulate and analyse the major ethical theories and approaches in the Western tradition in light of this shift. Such a broad historical perspective would allow students to apprehend why for instance, the preoccupation with the ‘Good’ gives rise to ethics of a particular ‘shape’, namely, ‘virtue ethics’; whereas the questions of ‘right’ and ‘wrong’, along with the procedural mode of their determination, emerge in the context of Enlightenment modernity, and the ‘disenchantment of nature’ that it brings in its wake. If ethics, under conditions of modernity, is compelled to take a more procedural form, as a reaction to ethical scepticism and the evisceration of ‘ethical content’ that the deracination of God from nature, hence of purposiveness in nature, entails, then the issue of what remains of the ‘old’ in the ‘new’, of the ancient in the modern, also surfaces. These themes would be pursued in different modalities, by raising, for instance, the problematic of the (privileged) ontological status of the ‘human’ (as opposed to the ‘animal’), in the modern discourse on ‘Human rights’ and environmental ethics.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Articulate and explain different Ethical theories and systems from a metaethical standpoint.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Critically analyse and evaluate these theories from the perspective of a broader intellectual history of ideas, identifying both their inner motivating sources and limitations.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Relate problems in ethics with specific issues in epistemology and ontology, such as (epistemic) skepcism and the (ontological) dualism between 'subject' and 'object'

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Apply existing ethical theories and arguments, as well as construct new approaches/ideas based on these theories, to contemporary issues, such as environmental ethics, anthropocentric/biocentric approaches, deep ecology etc.
